opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think compression is an interesting idea, and I understand why people are drawn to it. There's something intuitive about saying that if you can explain a lot of data with a small description, you must have understood something. But what's been bothering me is that compression, at least as it's usually measured, is blind to *how* the representation is organized internally. And I think that's where a lot of the real story is.

Here's the issue. You can have two systems that compress the same data to roughly the same degree. They produce the same outputs and get the same loss, so by the compression metric they look equivalent. But if you look inside, one of them might have a beautifully factored representation, where the underlying regularities of the world are carved at their joints. The other might be what we've been calling a fractured, entangled representation, where the same capability is implemented as a patchwork of special cases glued together in ways that happen to work on the data you've seen.

We saw this vividly in work with Picbreeder images. Those were images that people evolved through open-ended exploration. When you look at the networks underneath them, you find this remarkable modular structure. There will be one component that controls, say, the symmetry of a skull, and another that controls the mouth opening. If you move one weight, the mouth opens and closes coherently. Then you train a conventional network with SGD to output the exact same image, pixel for pixel. The output is identical, but the internal representation is a mess. Perturb it and you get garbage, not a meaningful variation. Both are, in some sense, compressed descriptions of that image, but they're not the same kind of understanding at all.

So my worry is that if we use compression as *the* measure of intelligence, we're measuring the wrong thing, or at least only a shadow of the right thing. What matters for intelligence, especially for creativity, generalization, and continual learning, is whether the representation is factored in a way that makes the next step easy. A good factoring means the space of adjacent possibilities is meaningful. If you nudge it, you get new ideas that make sense. A fractured representation can look just as compact, but it's a dead end. It doesn't open up the future.

And this connects to something I've cared about for a long time, which is that the *path* you take to a representation matters, not just where you end up. Picbreeder networks got their structure because they were built up incrementally through a process where each stepping stone was interesting in its own right. Regularities got locked in early and then elaborated on. Objective-driven optimization toward a fixed target doesn't respect that kind of history, so it can reach the same destination through a much uglier route.

So I wouldn't say compression is irrelevant. It's probably correlated with intelligence in some loose way. But I'd say it's insufficient. Two equally compressed representations can differ enormously in how much real understanding they embody, and the difference lies in the factoring. If we only look at the compression ratio or the benchmark score, we might be fooling ourselves into thinking we've built something that understands the world when what we've actually built is an impostor that happens to give the right answers.

r001.rationale: The response says equally compressed representations can differ in quality, favoring a well-factored representation over a fractured one with the same capability and compression.

r002.rationale: It describes components controlling skull symmetry and mouth opening, and says perturbing them can yield meaningful variations. It does not clearly state that factoring a face representation enables principled generation of new faces.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think compression is one of those ideas that sounds like it should capture intelligence, and in a certain sense it does, but I've come to believe that it misses something really important, which is what I'd call the factorization of the representation. So you can have two representations that compress to the same degree, the same number of bits, and they are not at all equivalent in terms of what they afford you.

Let me give you the intuition. Imagine you train a network to produce a particular image, and you train it with a conventional objective, and it eventually gets there. And then imagine a different network that was discovered through something like an open-ended process, like what we saw with Picbreeder, where people were just exploring and following their interests rather than trying to hit a target. Both networks can produce the same image. Both might even be about the same size. But if you look inside, the second one is factored in a way where the underlying regularities of the thing, say the symmetry of a face or the way the two eyes are tied together, are actually separated out into meaningful dimensions. You can tweak one weight and the mouth opens. You can tweak another and the whole thing rotates in a sensible way. Whereas in the conventionally trained one, you tweak a weight and you just get garbage. It's what I've been calling a fractured entangled representation versus a unified factored one.

So compression, as usually conceived, is blind to that difference. Kolmogorov complexity doesn't care whether the program is organized in a way that reflects the structure of the world. It only cares about length. And what that means is that you can be very compressed and still be very far from the kind of understanding that lets you generalize, be creative, continue learning, all the things we'd actually want from intelligence. I'd argue a representation that's slightly larger but properly factored is far more intelligent in any practical sense than one that's maximally compressed but entangled.

And I think this matters a lot right now because the field has largely gone with the assumption that if you scale up and optimize hard enough toward the objective, the good representation comes along for free, because it's the simplest explanation of the data. I'm skeptical of that. The order in which you learn things, the path you take through the search space, has an enormous effect on how the representation ends up organized. Deception in the objective, as we've talked about in the context of novelty search, means the direct path often leads you to a solution that works but is internally a mess. So I'd say compression is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The interesting question is not just how small the description is, but whether its parts correspond to the parts of the world.

r001.rationale: It says a slightly larger, properly factored representation can be more intelligent in practice than a maximally compressed but entangled one.

r002.rationale: It describes face-related factors such as symmetry and tied-together eyes, and says weights can change features or rotation. It does not clearly explain that these factors enable principled generation of new faces.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think compression captures something important, but it leaves open the question of how the representation is organized. You can have a very compact representation that makes the things you want to do incredibly difficult. So the amount of compression alone doesn't tell you how useful that representation is.

If you discover a good factorization, you're identifying things that can vary independently, or pieces that can be reused in different combinations. And that gives you more than an economical description of what you've already seen. It gives you a way to generate things you haven't seen, or to make a new problem easier to solve.

That's the part I'd want to understand before treating compression as a measure of intelligence. Does the representation expose useful structure? Does it make new possibilities accessible? Two representations could be similarly compressed and yet have very different consequences for what you can discover next.

r001.rationale: The response says compression alone can yield a representation that makes tasks difficult, while a good factorization exposes useful structure and makes new problems easier.

r002.rationale: It describes generating unseen things in general, but does not mention faces or explain how factoring a face representation enables new-face generation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compression captures something important, but you have to ask what the representation makes easy. You can have a very compact representation that is terrible for discovering anything new. And you can have a representation that looks redundant, but that exposes the factors you need to manipulate to solve a problem.

For example, imagine representing a picture as a list of pixels versus representing it as a collection of objects with positions and relationships. The second representation gives you handles on the world. You can ask what happens if an object moves, or combine familiar objects in a new arrangement. That’s useful beyond simply reconstructing the picture.

So the factoring matters enormously. Two representations might achieve similar compression while giving you completely different abilities to generalize or explore. From my perspective, a particularly interesting question is whether a representation opens up possibilities for future discovery. Compression may be part of that, but I don’t think the amount of compression, by itself, tells you whether you have the right building blocks.

r001.rationale: It says a representation that exposes factors for manipulation can be more useful than a compact one that makes discovery difficult.

r002.rationale: The response discusses objects and arrangements in pictures, but does not explain how factoring a face representation enables generating new faces.
